extracted.intended_audience: general readers and screenwriters seeking information on Syd Field and his screenwriting paradigm
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles derived from Syd Field's screenwriting paradigm, especially his three-act structure and its key plot milestones (inciting/plot point, midpoint, confrontation, resolution). Useful for writers assessing or structuring feature-length screenplays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-act structure (Field's paradigm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Field's most notable contribution is his paradigm 'three-act structure'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this structure, a writer sets a film's plot within the first twenty to thirty minutes. Then the protagonist experiences a plot point, providing the protagonist with a goal. About half of a movie's running time focuses on the protagonist's struggle to achieve this goal. The second act is called the confrontation. Field also refers to the midpoint, a turning point around the middle of the screenplay (such as on or around page 60 of a 120-page screenplay). This turning point is often a devastating reversal of the protagonist's fortune. The third act depicts the protagonist's struggle to achieve (or not achieve) his or her goal, as well as the aftermath.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set the film's plot within the first 20–30 minutes
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer should 'set a film's plot within the first twenty to thirty minutes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This early setup establishes the narrative framework and leads into the first major plot point; it orients the audience and introduces the situation that will be changed by the inciting plot point.

rubrics_metrics.name: First plot point must provide the protagonist with a goal
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist 'experiences a plot point, providing the protagonist with a goal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plot point functions as the inciting incident that turns the setup into an active quest; it should clearly define what the protagonist must attempt to achieve, driving the remainder of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second act as confrontation focusing on struggle
rubrics_metrics.description: The second act is called the 'confrontation' and occupies about half the movie's running time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roughly half the screenplay should center on the protagonist's efforts and obstacles in pursuing the goal set by the first plot point. This act should escalate conflict and complicate the protagonist's attempt to succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Midpoint as a major turning point (around page ~60 of 120)
rubrics_metrics.description: Field refers to the 'midpoint, a turning point around the middle of the screenplay (such as on or around page 60 of a 120-page screenplay).'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The midpoint is often a significant reversal or shift in the protagonist's fortunes; it should reorient the stakes or strategy and often forces a decisive change that propels the story into the second half of the confrontation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third act: struggle to achieve (or not) the goal and aftermath
rubrics_metrics.description: The third act 'depicts the protagonist's struggle to achieve (or not achieve) his or her goal, as well as the aftermath.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This act resolves the central conflict and shows consequences; it must deliver a satisfying outcome (success, failure, or bittersweet result) and tie up the narrative threads established earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Field's structural ideas as a measure of screenplay potential
rubrics_metrics.description: Hollywood film producers 'use Field's ideas on structure to measure the potential of screenplays.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adherence to Field's structural milestones (early setup, clear plot point/goal, midpoint reversal, sustained second-act confrontation, and coherent third-act resolution) is often treated as an indicator of a screenplay's commercial and dramatic viability.
